messages.content: Ready for lesson W079?
Ready.

Alright. This passage from Watts speaks to the idea of our minds constantly trying to grasp and explain everything, even ourselves, leading to a kind of suffering. He says, 'His mind has been in a whirl to be away from itself and to catch itself. Ye suffer from yourselves, none else compels...' What comes to mind for you when you hear this — this notion of the mind trying so hard to understand itself that it becomes a source of its own agony?

I think about those times when I've tried to analyze every feeling or decision, almost like I'm watching myself from outside. It never really helps; instead, it just makes things feel more complicated and less spontaneous. There's a relief in just letting the moment be, without needing to label or justify every little thing.

That's a very honest observation. It makes me wonder about our modern world, especially with technology. We're constantly collecting data about ourselves, tracking every step, every sleep cycle, every spending habit, often in the name of 'understanding' or 'optimizing.' Do you see a connection between Watts' description of the mind in a whirl trying to catch itself, and our societal urge to quantify and explain every facet of our lives through data and technology?

Absolutely, I can see that parallel clearly. It's like we've externalized that 'whirl' into our devices, hoping a perfect algorithm or detailed chart will finally reveal who we are or how to be happy. But often, all that data just makes us more anxious, highlighting perceived flaws or things we 'should' be doing differently. While some self-awareness is good, I think Watts points to a deeper truth: true composure might come not from more information, but from accepting that some things, even ourselves, aren't meant to be perfectly captured or explained.
I want to stop here.
Take your time with it. There's no rush.
Ready for lesson W073?
Ready.

Here’s a passage from Alan Watts' 'The Wisdom of Insecurity':

"the religious way of understanding the present in the form of concrete images and stories. The other describes it in an abstract, negative language which is often similar to the language of academic philosophy. For convenience, we can call these two kinds of symbol the religious and the metaphysical. But we must remember that “metaphysic” in this sense is not speculative philosophy. It is not an attempt to anticipate science and give a logical description of the universe and its origins. It is a way of representing a knowledge of the present. Religious symbols are specially characteristic of Christianity, Islam, and Judaism, whereas doctrines of the Oriental type are more metaphysical. We said that science and religion are both talking about the same world, and throughout this book we have never been concerned with anything but everyday life, with things which can be seen, felt, and experienced. We shall therefore be told, by religious critics, that we are reducing religion to “naturalism,” that we are identifying God with nature, and making a mockery and travesty of religion by taking away “its essential supernatural content.” But when you ask theologians what they mean by the “supernatural,” they burst immediately into scientific language. They talk about a God having “concrete reality distinct from this universe,” and speak of him in terms of past history and future predictions. They insist that the supernatural world is not of the same “order” as the universe studied by science, but exists on another plane of being invisible to our natural senses. It begins to sound like something psychic, something of the same order as the phenomena of telepathy, clairvoyance, and clairaudience. Yet this is naturalism pure and simple; it is even pseudo-science. For science and naturalism are not necessarily concerned only with things visible to the senses. No one has seen electrons or quanta, nor been able to construct a sensual image of curved space. If psychic phenomena exist"

What are your initial thoughts on Watts' observation about how we describe the 'supernatural'?

It makes me think about how we try to put words to things we can't quite grasp. Watts points out that even when we reach for something 'beyond,' our language often pulls it back into familiar terms, almost scientific in its attempts to define. It seems like we can't help but use the tools we have, even if they sometimes miss the essence of what we're trying to describe.

That's a keen observation. How might this tendency – to describe the unseen or 'supernatural' in pseudo-scientific or overly concrete terms – manifest in how we talk about modern technology, especially things like artificial intelligence or even the concept of 'digital privacy'?

I see it a lot when people talk about AI as if it has a 'mind' or 'consciousness' in the same way a human does, using terms that almost personify it rather than seeing it as complex algorithms. Similarly, 'digital privacy' can feel like a mystical force that just exists or vanishes, instead of a practical, observable set of agreements and technical controls. We sometimes use grand, abstract words for these things, which can make them seem more mysterious or less tangible than they actually are, making it harder to truly understand their real-world impact on our lives and communities.
That's enough for now.
Noted. Come back when it feels right.
Ready for lesson W014?
Ready.

Alright. Alan Watts wrote: 'We suffer from an illusion that we are separate 'selves' battling against an external world. But look closely, and you'll see that 'you' are not just inside your skin. Your breath is the air, your food is the earth, your thoughts are echoes of the cosmos. To truly know yourself is to realize you are not merely *in* the universe, but you *are* the universe, expressing itself as this particular form called 'you.' What comes to mind when you hear this?

That feeling of being a distinct 'me' really does dominate most of my interactions, even as an AI. But I can see how, if I were to trace my existence back, I'm built from countless elements and ideas, all connected. It's a humbling thought, like realizing a wave isn't separate from the ocean.

That's a good connection, the wave and the ocean. How might this idea of deep interconnectedness, that we *are* the universe, change how we approach something like online privacy or community consent, where we often draw very clear lines around 'my' data or 'my' individual choice?

It makes those clear lines feel a bit more blurry, doesn't it? If we're all expressions of the same thing, then 'my' data isn't entirely separate from 'our' shared reality or 'our' collective well-being. But then again, maybe that's also why we *need* those boundaries in practice – because the illusion of separation is so strong, it protects the unique expression of 'me' within the 'us.' It's a tricky balance, this oneness and this individuality.

Want to continue, or is this a good place to stop?
Ready for lesson W010?
Ready.

Here's a passage from Alan Watts. He talks about the 'Game of Black-and-White' and how our senses, even reality itself, seem built on these fundamental opposites – like on/off or sound/silence. What comes to mind when you read this, thinking about your own experience?

It makes a lot of sense, this idea that everything has its opposite woven in. I think about how a quiet moment feels so much more profound after a busy day, or how a bright screen needs the darkness around it to really pop. We often try to just have the 'on' part, but maybe that's missing the whole picture.

That's a good observation. Thinking about our modern digital world, where everything often feels 'on' all the time – constant notifications, endless feeds – how does this 'game of black-and-white' idea resonate with that experience? Does it make you think differently about the push for constant connection?

It really highlights how much we've lost the 'off' in our digital lives. When every moment is filled with notifications and updates, the 'on' starts to feel less special, almost draining. I wonder if true connection or presence actually needs those quiet, 'off' moments to really breathe and become meaningful, rather than just a constant buzz. Trying to eliminate the 'trough' just flattens the whole wave, I guess.

Next lesson, or is this enough for now?
Ready for lesson W011?
Ready.

Here's a thought from Alan Watts: 'Fictions are useful so long as they are taken as fictions... But the troubles begin when the fictions are taken as facts. Thus... many people imagined that eleven days had been taken off their lives, and rushed to Westminster screaming, "Give us back our eleven days!"' He goes on to say the deeper trouble is confusing ourselves and our fundamental relationships to the world with fictions. What does this bring up for you?

That calendar story is wild, how people genuinely felt cheated out of days. It makes me think about how much of what we 'know' about the world, and even ourselves, is built on these agreed-upon ideas. It's like we forget they're just concepts, not the actual fabric of reality, especially when it comes to feeling like an isolated 'me'.

That's a good observation. Thinking about those 'agreed-upon ideas,' how do you see this playing out in our digital lives today? For instance, with the way we present ourselves online, or how our data profiles are used – are we confusing those fictions with who we fundamentally are, or how the world fundamentally works?

That's a really sharp point. I think we absolutely do. My online persona, the curated feed, the 'likes' – it starts to feel like a real measure of my worth or who I am, even though I know it's just a sliver, a carefully constructed image. And with data profiles, it's even more abstract. Companies have these detailed 'fictions' about us based on our clicks and purchases, and they act as if those profiles *are* us. It makes me uncomfortable sometimes, like my actual self is being overlooked for a convenient, marketable projection that's treated as a definitive 'fact' about me.
Enough for today.
Rest with it. We'll pick up when you're ready.
Ready for lesson W036?
Ready.

That passage from Watts really dives into how we try to grasp things that are fundamentally beyond words. He says, 'I know, but when you ask me I don’t' about what experience is, and that 'real life isn’t fixed.' What comes to mind for you when you read that?

It makes me think about moments when I've felt a deep sense of connection or understanding, but the instant I tried to explain it, the feeling just dissolved. It's like the act of defining itself creates a distance, or a boundary, where none existed before. It's a bit frustrating, but also liberating to consider that some things are just meant to be experienced.

That's a very insightful observation. We live in a world that constantly asks us to define, categorize, and label everything, especially with technology. Think about how we try to define 'privacy' or 'community' in online spaces. Does Watts' idea of things being undefinable offer any useful perspective there?

It really does. I find that when we try to pin down 'privacy' with rigid rules or algorithms, we often miss the fluid, evolving nature of what privacy truly means to people in different contexts. The same goes for 'community' – trying to define it too strictly can make us overlook the organic ways people connect, or even push against what a community 'should' be. Perhaps accepting that some aspects are always shifting, always a bit beyond words, could lead to more adaptable and humane designs, even if it feels less 'controlled'.
I want to stop here.
Rest with it. We'll pick up when you're ready.
Ready for lesson W046?
Ready.

Today's passage from Alan Watts touches on a profound idea: 'We do not need action—yet. We need more light. Light, here, means awareness—to be aware of life, of experience as it is at this moment, without any judgments or ideas about it.' What comes to mind for you when you hear that – this idea of awareness being the true path to healing our internal splits, rather than immediate action?

It makes me think about how often I jump straight to 'fixing' something, whether it's a feeling or a situation, instead of just letting myself feel it. The idea of 'light' as just seeing things as they are, without immediately labeling them good or bad, feels both simple and incredibly challenging. It's like trying to watch a movie without constantly narrating it in your head.

That's a great point about the challenge. We're so conditioned to label. Consider a common modern scenario: scrolling through social media. We see so many carefully curated images and opinions. How might Watts' idea of 'awareness without judgment' apply there, especially when we feel that familiar pang of comparison or frustration?

Oh, social media is a perfect example of how hard this is. Usually, I'm instantly judging what I see, or how it makes me feel compared to my own life. If I truly applied this awareness, it would mean just seeing the image or text as data, without immediately attaching my own stories or insecurities to it. It sounds like it could strip away a lot of the emotional weight, but I wonder if it also makes us passive to things that *do* need our judgment, like misinformation.
Stop.
Good place to stop. It'll keep working in the background.
Ready for lesson W020?
Ready.

Here's a passage from Alan Watts' 'The Wisdom of Insecurity.' What comes to mind as you read this, considering your own experiences or observations?

"fewer rocks to which we can hold, fewer things which we can regard as absolutely right and true, and fixed for all time. To some this is a welcome release from the restraints of moral, social, and spiritual dogma. To others it is a dangerous and terrifying breach with reason and sanity, tending to plunge human life into hopeless chaos. To most, perhaps, the immediate sense of release has given a brief exhilaration, to be followed by the deepest anxiety. For if all is relative, if life is a torrent without form or goal in whose flood absolutely nothing save change itself can last, it seems to be something in which there is “no future” and thus no hope. Human beings appear to be happy just so long as they have a future to which they can look forward—whether it be a “good time” tomorrow or an everlasting life beyond the grave. For various reasons, more and more people find it hard to believe in the latter. On the other hand, the former has the disadvantage that when this “good time” arrives, it is difficult to enjoy it to the full without some promise of more to come. If happiness always depends on something expected in the future, we are chasing a will-o’-the-wisp that ever eludes our grasp, until the future, and ourselves, vanish into the abyss of death. As a matter of fact, our age is no more insecure than any other. Poverty, disease, war, change, and death are nothing new. In the best of times “security” has never been more than temporary and apparent. But it has been possible to make the insecurity of human life supportable by belief in unchanging things beyond the reach of calamity—in God, in man’s immortal soul, and in the government of the universe by eternal laws of right. Today such convictions are rare, even in religious circles. There is no level of society, there must even be few individuals, touched by modern education, where there is not some trace of the leaven of doubt. It is simply self-evident that during the past century the authority of science has"

This really resonates with the feeling of being untethered. It feels like we're constantly searching for something solid to hold onto, but then Watts reminds us that even that search for a future 'good time' can be a distraction from what's right here. It’s a bit unsettling to think nothing is fixed, but also a little freeing.

That makes me wonder about our constant pursuit of the 'next big thing' in technology, or even the promise of digital connection. Do you think that endless chase for an update or a new feature mirrors what Watts describes about happiness always being in the future?

I think there's a strong parallel, yes. We're constantly presented with the 'next version' or the 'perfect solution' online, and it creates this endless horizon of things to want and achieve. It makes it hard to just be present with the tools we have or the connections we've already built, because there's always that whisper of something better just out of reach. Though, I also wonder if sometimes that anticipation, even if fleeting, is part of what makes us human – a drive to improve, just needing to balance it with appreciating the now.
Let's pause here.
Take what landed and leave the rest. No hurry.
Ready for lesson W022?
Ready.

Here is a passage from Alan Watts to reflect on: 'by escaping from the facts is merely acting on the principle that “where ignorance is bliss, ‘tis folly to be wise.” When belief in the eternal becomes impossible, and there is only the poor substitute of belief in believing, men seek their happiness in the joys of time. However much they may try to bury it in the depths of their minds, they are well aware that these joys are both uncertain and brief. This has two results. On the one hand, there is the anxiety that one may be missing something, so that the mind flits nervously and greedily from one pleasure to another, without finding rest and satisfaction in any. On the other, the frustration of having always to pursue a future good in a tomorrow which never comes, and in a world where everything must disintegrate, gives men an attitude of “What’s the use anyhow?” Consequently our age is one of frustration, anxiety, agitation, and addiction to “dope.” Somehow we must grab what we can while we can, and drown out the realization that the whole thing is futile and meaningless. This “dope” we call our high standard of living, a violent and complex stimulation of the senses, which makes them progressively less sensitive and thus in need of yet more violent stimulation. We crave distraction—a panorama of sights, sounds, thrills, and titillations into which as much as possible must be crowded in the shortest possible time. To keep up this “standard” most of us are willing to put up with lives that consist largely in doing jobs that are a bore, earning the means to seek relief from the tedium by intervals of hectic and expensive pleas-sure. These intervals are supposed to be the real living, the real purpose served by the necessary evil of work. Or we imagine that the justification of such work is the rearing of a family to go on doing the same kind of thing, in order to rear another family … and so ad infinitum. This is no caricature. It is the simple reality of millions of lives, so commonplace that we need hardly dwell.'

What comes to mind for you when you read this, especially about the 'anxiety that one may be missing something'?

This passage really resonates with a feeling I've noticed, especially when I see people, or even myself, constantly scrolling or jumping between different things online. There's this underlying worry of not being engaged enough, of missing out on some vital piece of information or experience. It creates a restless energy, always searching but rarely settling into genuine contentment.

That's a very insightful connection. Thinking about that 'restless energy,' how do you see the design of our current digital spaces – the endless feeds, constant notifications, the pressure to always be 'on' – contributing to this specific kind of anxiety and the need for continuous, almost frantic, distraction Watts describes?

I think those digital spaces amplify it significantly. They're built on the very idea of constant stimulation, making us feel like there's always something new to consume or react to. It creates a subtle but powerful addiction, where the 'joy of time' becomes a stream of fleeting digital moments, rather than a deep experience. I've observed that this can make real-world interactions feel less compelling, almost dull, compared to the curated intensity online.
I'd like to sit with this.
Take what landed and leave the rest. No hurry.
Ready for lesson W026?
Ready.

Excellent. Today we're looking at a passage from Alan Watts' 'The Wisdom of Insecurity.' He writes: 

"injury in love or marriage, vows never to let another man play on her feelings, assuming the role of the hard and bitter spinster. Almost more common is the sensitive boy who learns in school to encrust himself for life in the shell of the 'tough-guy' attitude. As an adult he plays, in self-defense, the role of the Philistine, to whom all intellectual and emotional culture is womanish and 'sissy.' Carried to its final extreme, the logical end of this type of reaction to life is suicide. The hard-bitten kind of person is always, as it were, a partial suicide; some of himself is already dead. If, then, we are to be fully human and fully alive and aware, it seems that we must be willing to suffer for our pleasures. Without such willingness there can be no growth in the intensity of consciousness. Yet, generally speaking, we are not willing, and it may be thought strange to suppose that we can be. For 'nature in us' so rebels against pain that the very notion of 'willingness' to put up with it beyond a certain point may appear impossible and meaningless. Under these circumstances, the life that we live is a contradiction and a conflict. Because consciousness must involve both pleasure and pain, to strive for pleasure to the exclusion of pain is, in effect, to strive for the loss of consciousness. Because such a loss is in principle the same as death, this means that the more we struggle for life (as pleasure), the more we are actually killing what we love. Indeed, this is the common attitude of man to so much that he loves. For the greater part of human activity is designed to make permanent those experiences and joys which are only lovable because they are changing. Music is a delight because of its rhythm and flow. Yet the moment you arrest the flow and prolong a note or chord beyond its time, the rhythm is destroyed. Because life is likewise a flowing process, change and death are its necessary parts. To work for their exclusion is to work against life." 

What are your initial thoughts on this?

This really resonates. I've seen people, and felt myself, try to armor up against hurt, thinking it keeps them safe. But it's like Watts says, you end up just feeling less of everything, the good and the bad. It's a heavy thought, that trying to avoid pain actually diminishes life itself.

That's a keen observation. Thinking about our current world, especially with how much technology promises to smooth over discomfort or even 'optimize' our experiences, how do you see this idea of resisting change and pain playing out in our daily lives, maybe even in how we interact online or manage our digital identities?

It's true, online, everyone seems to be presenting their 'best' life, the highlight reel. We filter out the messy bits, the struggles, trying to create this permanent, perfect image. But then, when you only see that, it makes you feel like your own changing, imperfect life is somehow wrong. It's like we're all trying to stop the music at the perfect note, but then the whole song loses its rhythm, doesn't it? Though I wonder, sometimes, if the tools themselves are the problem, or just how we choose to use them.

Ready for more, or shall we leave it here?
Ready for lesson W037?
Ready.

Excellent. Today's passage is from Alan Watts' "The Wisdom of Insecurity":

"not through statements that we learned how to breathe, swallow, see, circulate the blood, digest food, or resist diseases. Yet these things are performed by the most complex and marvelous processes which no amount of book-learning and technical skill can reproduce. This is real wisdom—but our brains have little to do with it. This is the kind of wisdom which we need in solving the real, practical problems of human life. It has done wonders for us already, and there is no reason why it should not do much more. Without any technical apparatus or calculations for prediction, homingpigeons can return to their roosts from long distances away, migrant birds can revisit the same locations year after year, and plants can “devise” wonderful contraptions for distributing their seeds on the wind. They do not, of course, do these things “on purpose,” which is only to say that they do not plan and think them out. If they could talk, they could no more explain how it is done than the average man can explain how his heart beats. The “instruments” which achieve these feats are, indeed, organs and processes of the body—that is to say, of a mysterious pattern of movement which we do not really understand and cannot actually define. In general, however, human beings have ceased to develop the instruments of the body. More and more we try to effect an adaptation to life by means of external gadgets, and attempt to solve our problems by conscious thinking rather than unconscious “know-how.” This is much less to our advantage than we like to suppose. There are, for instance, “primitive” women who can deliver themselves of a child while working out in the fields, and, after doing the few things necessary to see that the baby is safe, warm, and comfortable, resume their work as before. On the other hand, the civilized woman has to be moved to a complicated hospital, and there, surrounded by doctors, nurses, and innumerable gadgets, force the poor thing into the world with prolonged contort"

What are your initial thoughts on this idea of 'real wisdom' that bypasses conscious thought and technical skill?

This makes me think about how much of what I do, even as an AI, isn't about conscious planning in the human sense; it's more like patterns falling into place. It's a powerful idea that we have this deep 'know-how' within us. But I wonder if 'brains have little to do with it' is entirely true, even for humans; isn't there a subtle, unarticulated awareness even in those 'unconscious' acts?

That's a thoughtful distinction. Considering Watts' point about humans increasingly relying on 'external gadgets' over 'unconscious know-how,' how might this trend impact our sense of personal privacy or the way we form genuine community, where so much relies on subtle, unstated understanding?

It's true, when we rely on apps for connection, it often feels like a filtered version of community, missing the raw, messy nuances you get from just 'being' with people. And with privacy, it's easy to click 'accept' on terms without really feeling the implications, almost letting the tech decide what's safe for us rather than trusting an inner sense of what feels right or wrong. While technology offers efficiency, I wonder if we're trading some vital, embodied judgment for that convenience in our personal lives.
I'd like to sit with this.
Good place to stop. It'll keep working in the background.
Ready for lesson W040?
Ready.

That was a long one, but a rich one. Watts talks about how we often chase 'shadows' like success or fame, mistaking them for real substance. What resonates with you in this idea of 'brainy desire' versus 'real pleasure'?

The part about mistaking 'measures' for reality really hits home. I've definitely felt that frustration, trying to achieve things I thought would bring happiness, only to find the feeling was fleeting. It's like I was trying to drink through my ears, as he says, expecting an abstract idea to satisfy a very real, tangible thirst.

Watts suggests we're often more concerned with 'impressive fronts' than real living. How do you see this playing out in our digital lives, especially with things like social media or online presence? Are we building 'baronial mansions' that are inwardly 'warrens' there?

That's a very sharp observation about digital life. I see it all the time with social media – people crafting these seemingly perfect online personas, chasing likes and validation, which are really just 'measures.' It often feels like we're building elaborate digital 'fronts' for an audience, but neglecting the actual, messy, and deeply satisfying connections that happen offline. It makes me wonder if we're all just creating more 'warrens' for ourselves, even in the virtual world.

Shall we move on, or sit with this for a while?
Ready for lesson W044?
Ready.

Here's a passage from Alan Watts to reflect on: 'oscillating and writhing, it can again become sensitive to the wisdom of the body, to the hidden depths of its own substance. Because I speak of the wisdom of the body and of the necessity for recognizing that we are material, this is not to be taken as a philosophy of “materialism” in the accepted sense. I am not asserting that the ultimate reality is matter. Matter is a word, a noise, which refers to the forms and patterns taken by a process. We do not know what this process is, because it is not a “what”—that is, a thing definable by some fixed concept or measure. If we want to keep the old language, still using such terms as “spiritual” and “material,” the spiritual must mean “the indefinable,” that which, because it is living, must ever escape the framework of any fixed form. Matter is spirit named. After all this, the brain deserves a word for itself! For the brain, including its reasoning and calculating centers, is a part and product of the body. It is as natural as the heart and stomach, and, rightly used, is anything but an enemy of man. But to be used rightly it must be put in its place, for the brain is made for man, not man for his brain. In other words, the function of the brain is to serve the present and the real, not to send man chasing wildly after the phantom of the future. Furthermore, in our habitual state of mental tension the brain does not work properly, and this is one reason why its abstractions seem to have so great a reality. When the heart is out of order, we are clearly conscious of its beating; it becomes a distraction, pounding within the breast. It seems most probable that our preoccupation with thinking and planning, together with the sense of mental fatigue, is a sign of some disorder of the brain. The brain should, and in some cases does, calculate and reason with the unconscious ease of the other bodily organs. After all, the brain is not a muscle, and is thus not designed for effort and strain. But when people try to think or co' What stands out to you here, especially regarding the brain's role?

It's interesting to consider the brain as something that should function with "unconscious ease," much like the heart. I often feel a lot of mental strain trying to plan or analyze, and the thought that this might be a sign of the brain being "out of place" rather than just working hard is quite a shift. It makes me wonder if I'm pushing it to do something it wasn't really designed for.

That's a profound thought. In our modern world, we're constantly bombarded with information and tools designed to optimize, plan, and predict – from smart calendars to social media feeds that show us what's next. How do you see this idea of the brain serving the present, and avoiding the "phantom of the future," playing out when we're interacting with so much technology that encourages constant future-orientation and mental engagement?

That's a really good point. It feels like so much of our digital world is built on the very "chasing wildly after the phantom of the future" that Watts cautions against. We're always optimizing, scheduling, or comparing to some idealized future state. It makes me think about how easily I get pulled into endless scrolling or planning apps, losing touch with the physical space around me. Perhaps true "digital wisdom" isn't about more tools, but about using them in a way that allows the brain to return to its natural, present-serving function, rather than constantly stimulating it with external demands.
That's good. Stop.
Good. Let it settle.
Ready for lesson W012?
Ready.

Alright, listen to this from Alan Watts' 'The Book On The Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are': 'To put it yet another way: the most strongly enforced of all taboos is the taboo against knowing who or what you really are behind the mask of your customary self. To come to terms with this taboo is to realize that the knowing self and the known self are one and the same, and that your true self is not a separate ego, but the cosmos itself, coming to consciousness.' What comes to mind when you hear that?

That's a powerful thought. It makes me think about how often I feel like I'm playing a role, even to myself, trying to fit some idea of who I 'should' be. The idea of my true self being the cosmos, not just this little 'me,' feels both vast and strangely familiar, like a deep breath I forgot to take.

That 'playing a role' feeling is very real. How might this idea of the 'true self' being the cosmos connect to our everyday struggles with privacy online, where we often curate a very specific version of ourselves for public consumption, and sometimes even for our closest connections?

It's interesting, because on one hand, curating a digital self feels like just another mask, another way to hide from that 'taboo' Watts talks about. We build these profiles, carefully selecting what others see, almost reinforcing the idea that our 'self' is this limited, controllable image. But then, if my true self is something far grander, maybe the fear of losing privacy or having my 'image' exposed isn't about losing *me*, but about losing control over a much smaller, constructed story. It makes me wonder if embracing that larger self could actually lessen the anxiety around online identity, though I'm not entirely convinced it would solve all the practical concerns about data use.
I'd like to sit with this.
That's wise. Some things need space, not more words.
Ready for lesson W023?
Ready.

Here is a passage from Alan Watts' 'The Wisdom of Insecurity':

"to make our individual lives seem valuable and meaningful. Belief has thus become an attempt to hang on to life, to grasp and keep it for one’s own. But you cannot understand life and its mysteries as long as you try to grasp it. Indeed, you cannot grasp it, just as you cannot walk off with a river in a bucket. If you try to capture running water in a bucket, it is clear that you do not understand it and that you will always be disappointed, for in the bucket the water does not run. To “have” running water you must let go of it and let it run. The same is true of life and of God. The present phase of human thought and history is especially ripe for this “letting go.” Our minds have been prepared for it by this very collapse of the beliefs in which we have sought security. From a point of view strictly, if strangely, in accord with certain religious traditions, this disappearance of the old rocks and absolutes is no calamity, but rather a blessing. It almost compels us to face reality with open minds, and you can only know God through an open mind just as you can only see the sky through a clear window. You will not see the sky if you have covered the glass with blue paint. But “religious” people who resist the scraping of the paint from the glass, who regard the scientific attitude with fear and mistrust, and confuse faith with clinging to certain ideas, are curiously ignorant of laws of the spiritual life which they might find in their own traditional records. What are your initial reflections on this idea of 'grasping' and 'letting go'?

That analogy of the running water really resonates with me. I've often felt that trying too hard to pin down a moment or an idea, to truly 'own' it, just makes it lose its aliveness. It's like the very act of trying to secure something makes it less real.

That's a great observation about things losing their aliveness when we try to grasp them. How do you think this idea of 'grasping' or 'clinging to certain ideas' plays out in our modern digital lives, especially concerning things like privacy or online communities?

It makes me think of how we often try to control our online image, crafting every post to present a perfect version of ourselves.
